passage: When Vidya joined our section in August, I thought she was being rude. Somebody said Mr Pai's surprise test was "very season two", the whole row groaned in agreement, and Vidya just said, "Harish, what does that even mean?" It's from a web series everyone watched last year, where season two ruined everything. You say it when something good turns bad. I explained it, feeling like an old man. Two weeks later I called her drawing "mid", meaning it was good, the way my group uses it. She went silent for the rest of biology. Turns out at her old school in Chennai, "mid" meant boring, basically an insult. I had to explain myself again, this time with my ears burning. Now we keep a list on the back page of her rough book: our words, her words, and what they meant last month. Half of them are already out of date.

qa.q: What does 'very season two' mean in Harish's class?
qa.a: You say it when something good turns bad, after a web series where season two ruined everything.

qa.q: How did Harish feel explaining 'mid' the second time?
qa.a: Harish felt embarrassed, ears burning, and probably a little guilty for hurting Vidya with a word meant as praise.

qa.q: What could someone do when a newcomer misses group slang?
qa.a: Explain it plainly without teasing, and check what words mean where the other person comes from, like the list on the back page of the rough book.

qa.q: What was it like for Vidya to hear 'very season two' in her first days?
qa.a: Vidya was left outside a joke the whole row shared, so all she could do was ask what it meant while everyone else groaned together.

grounding: It shows references and slang signalling group membership, a newcomer missing them, and the same word meaning different things in different groups.

passage: The Sunday before my boards, Alka came over "for ten minutes" and was still on my bed at eight, scrolling short videos and narrating each one. I had two chapters left. So I did what my mother does with guests. "It's getting late, na?" I said, looking at the clock. Alka said, "Arre, it's only eight," and played another one. I yawned, loudly. I started stacking my books on the desk. I even said, "Tomorrow is going to be so long." She said, "Same," and settled deeper into my pillow. By nine I was annoyed enough to snap, and I could feel it building. Instead I said, "Alka, I need you to go now so I can study. Pani puri after the exam?" She jumped up. "Anjali, why didn't you just say? I thought you wanted company." Honestly, I thought I had said it. About five times.

qa.q: How many chapters did Anjali have left?
qa.a: Anjali had two chapters left.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling by nine?
qa.a: Anjali was annoyed and stressed about the unfinished chapters, close to snapping; there may also have been some guilt about pushing Alka out.

qa.q: What finally worked, and why?
qa.a: A clear request with a reason and a later plan, 'I need you to go now so I can study', worked because Alka had missed every hint. 👍

qa.q: How did Alka read the evening?
qa.a: Alka thought Anjali wanted company, so the yawns and 'it's getting late' just sounded like ordinary chatting.

grounding: It shows hints like 'it's getting late' saving face but going unnoticed, and a clear request ending the confusion.

passage: It took me a while to understand why the jokes at coaching made my stomach knot. Whenever I drew a graph on the board, Nitin would say, "Nice curves, Himani," in a normal voice, as if he meant the maths. The back row snickered every time, and he looked at me, not at the board. The first week I laughed along because I wasn't sure. Was it about the graph? Was I being dramatic? But my shoulders went up every time I picked up the marker. The second week I turned round and said, "That's not okay. Stop." He put his hands up: "Relax, it's about parabolas." On Friday he said it again. That evening I stayed back and told Kavitha Ma'am everything, including the part I'd laughed at. She didn't ask whether I'd misheard. She said, "You were right to tell me," called Nitin's father that same evening, and moved him to the other batch from Monday.

qa.q: What did Nitin say when Himani drew a graph?
qa.a: He said, "Nice curves, Himani," in a normal voice.

qa.q: How did Himani feel each time the marker came out?
qa.a: Himani felt uncomfortable and tense, shoulders going up, and unsure whether the remark was really about maths; wondering about 'being dramatic' shows confusion mixed with hurt.

qa.q: Which steps helped Himani, and why?
qa.a: Himani said 'That's not okay. Stop', and when it continued told Kavitha Ma'am everything; she believed Himani, called Nitin's father that evening and moved him to another batch.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha Ma'am had asked whether Himani misheard?
qa.a: Himani might have felt doubted and blamed, and the remarks could have carried on without anyone stopping them.

grounding: It shows a teenager noticing the suggestive second meaning in a remark, saying it is not okay, and telling a trusted adult when it continues.

passage: Twenty minutes before the relatives were due for Lakshmi puja, the power went out across the colony, and Dadi was already tense. Neelam was lighting diyas by phone torch when she finally said it. "Dadi, why do we do the whole aarti in Sanskrit if none of us understands it?" Dadi's hands paused on the thali. Neelam's cousin hissed, "Not now." Zubin, from next door, who had come to borrow candles, looked at the floor. Neelam lowered her voice. "I'm not saying stop. I'll do it. I just want it to mean something to me." Dadi was quiet, then handed her the last diya. "Your Dada used to say the prayer twice, once in Sanskrit, once in Hindi, for the children. Do it his way." In the dark, with the torch shaking, Neelam said both. On his way out Zubin said softly, "We ask the same questions at the fire temple. My grandmother hates it too."

qa.q: What did Neelam's Dada use to do with the prayer?
qa.a: He said it twice, once in Sanskrit and once in Hindi, for the children.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when asking about the Sanskrit aarti?
qa.a: Neelam was probably frustrated and a bit disconnected, wanting the ritual to mean something; the lowered voice shows worry about hurting Dadi too.

qa.q: Which choice helped keep both the ritual and the question?
qa.a: Neelam said she would still take part and only wanted meaning, and Dadi offered Dada's way of praying in both languages, so questioning and joining in could coexist.

qa.q: What was it like for Dadi when the question came during the power cut?
qa.a: Dadi was already tense and her hands paused, so she likely felt challenged, but she answered with a family memory instead of pressure.

grounding: It shows a teenager respectfully questioning a ritual and finding personal meaning in it while still taking part, with no pressure from either side.

subtype: Reverence and respect in shared spaces [Expressing]
passage: The rain came down so hard on the school heritage walk that the group scattered, and Gautam and Tanuja ended up alone at the gate of the old gurdwara, soaked and without their teacher. "Can we just wait inside?" Tanuja whispered. Gautam hesitated at the steps. Everyone around them was slipping off their shoes into the racks and rinsing their feet in a shallow channel of water. He copied them, then noticed every head was covered, even a toddler's. He had nothing. He went up to an older man handing out tea and asked quietly, "Sorry, uncle, I'm visiting. Is it okay to come in, and do I need to cover my head?" The man smiled and pulled two orange cloths from a basket. "Both of you. Welcome." Inside, the hymns were soft and steady. Gautam sat cross-legged near the back, dripping, and didn't take out his phone once. When the teacher's call finally came, he stepped outside before answering.

qa.q: What did the older man pull from the basket?
qa.a: He pulled two orange cloths from a basket.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he hesitated at the steps?
qa.a: Gautam felt unsure and a bit nervous about getting unfamiliar customs wrong, while wanting to be respectful; it might also have been shyness about being soaked and alone.

qa.q: How did Gautam work out what to do?
qa.a: He watched the people around him and copied the shoes and foot rinsing, then asked politely about covering his head instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might the older man have seen the two soaked visitors?
qa.a: The man seemed glad they asked, smiling and handing both of them cloths, so he likely saw them as respectful guests.

grounding: It shows a teenager showing respect in an unfamiliar place of worship by removing shoes, covering the head and staying quiet, learning by watching and politely asking.

subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage:
Zubin: uma I think I messed up in class today 😅
Uma: the palm thing?
Zubin: yes. I was trying to say I'd finished the homework and you looked so confused
Uma: your handshape was perfect. but your palm faced you instead of out, so it became a different sign
Zubin: wait, the direction alone changes it?
Uma: yes. like changing a vowel in a spoken word. it's grammar, not decoration
Zubin: I thought you'd get the idea from the gist
Uma: sometimes. but lots of hearing learners treat signs like loose gestures. it's tiring to keep guessing what they mean
Zubin: that's fair. sorry. can you check me before class tomorrow?
Uma: yes. 10 mins early, library corner. bring a video of yourself signing
Zubin: deal. palm out. palm OUT 🙏

qa.q: What was wrong with Zubin's sign?
qa.a: Zubin's palm faced inward instead of out, so it became a different sign.

qa.q: What might Uma feel when learners treat signs like loose gestures?
qa.a: Uma seems tired and a little frustrated at having to keep guessing; still, offering to check Zubin before class shows patience and care.

qa.q: What small step will help Zubin?
qa.a: Practising with Uma ten minutes early and bringing a video of the signing helps Zubin check palm direction instead of relying on the gist.

qa.q: What would change if Zubin kept treating palm direction as a detail?
qa.a: Zubin's signs would keep turning into different words, so partners like Uma would have to guess and the conversation would break down.

grounding: It shows that the direction a palm faces changes a sign's meaning like a vowel changes a word, and a hearing learner coming to respect that grammar.

passage: At the Thursday market in the kasba, Sudha helped Jyoti at the bangle stall and practised the signs Jyoti had been teaching her for months. That afternoon Jyoti's cousin Mitali arrived from Khulna, across the border, and the two of them signed so fast that Sudha's head spun. She watched their hands, then remembered what Jyoti always told her: watch the face too. Mitali's eyebrows went up and her hand moved forward through the space between them; Jyoti's mouth pulled tight. Sudha guessed it was bad news, then caught herself. Some of Mitali's handshapes looked nothing like the ones Jyoti used. She tapped Jyoti's arm and signed slowly, "Sorry. Again, slower, please?" Jyoti laughed and switched to signs Sudha knew: Mitali's bus had broken down and she had walked three kilometres. Not bad news; tired news. "Her signing is from Bangladesh," Jyoti signed. "Different signs. But you watched her face. Good."

qa.q: Where did Mitali come from?
qa.a: Mitali came from Khulna, across the border.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling while watching the fast signing?
qa.a: Sudha felt overwhelmed and a bit anxious, head spinning; seeing Jyoti's tight mouth, Sudha guessed bad news, though it turned out to be tiredness.

qa.q: Which choice helped Sudha understand?
qa.a: Instead of guessing from faces, Sudha tapped Jyoti's arm and asked for it again, slower, so Jyoti could explain in familiar signs.

qa.q: How might Mitali's arrival have looked from Jyoti's side?
qa.a: For Jyoti it was a cousin arriving tired after a long walk, and she was happy to switch to signs Sudha knew so everyone could follow.

grounding: It shows a learner following a signed conversation by watching hands, space and faces, asking for repetition instead of guessing, and meeting signing from another country.

passage: At the district school's Language Day, the hall was packed and noisy. When Shalini's turn came, she walked to the centre of the stage without a mic. Shalini is Deaf, and her interpreter, Mrs Bose, stood at the side to voice. Shalini signed a poem about her grandmother's kitchen: hands shaping steam, a rolling pin, a slap on the wrist for stealing jaggery. Her face did half the work, and the front rows laughed a beat before Mrs Bose's voice caught up. At the end, a row of deaf students waved both hands in the air instead of clapping, and Shalini waved back, grinning. Next was Deepak, who is hard of hearing and wears hearing aids. He spoke his poem in Bengali, clear and slow. Backstage a teacher asked him, "Why don't you sign too?" Deepak shrugged. "I sign with friends. On stage I like my voice." Shalini, catching it, bumped his shoulder. "Both are proper," she signed.

qa.q: What was Shalini's poem about?
qa.a: It was about her grandmother's kitchen.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the row waved both hands?
qa.a: Shalini felt proud and happy, grinning and waving back; being seen by other signers probably felt like belonging, not just applause. 😊

qa.q: How did the event support both students' choices?
qa.a: It gave Shalini an interpreter so she could perform in sign and let Deepak speak, so each could present in the language they chose.

qa.q: How might Deepak see the teacher's question?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt his choice was being questioned, but he answered calmly that he signs with friends and likes his voice on stage.

grounding: It shows a Deaf teenager taking pride in signing and a hard-of-hearing peer choosing speech on stage, with both treated as complete, valid choices.

passage:
Dear Rekha Ma'am,
Thank you for the comments on my essay about banning single-use plastic in the canteen. You wrote, "Your evidence is strong, but you sound furious at the reader." I didn't believe you, so I read it aloud to my brother, and at "anyone who disagrees is simply lazy" he said, "Ouch, so I'm lazy now?" You were right. On paper nobody can see me smiling. So I have redrafted it. My thesis is now one plain sentence at the top. I kept the canteen waste count from our survey, 140 cups a day, and added the counterargument you asked for: steel tumblers cost money and need washing. I answer that with the parent volunteer rota. I replaced "lazy" with "understandably busy", and "obviously" now appears zero times instead of seven. Could you look at the new version before Friday? I've attached it.
Regards,
Nandini

qa.q: How many cups a day did the survey count?
qa.a: The survey counted 140 cups a day.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when the brother said 'Ouch, so I'm lazy now?'
qa.a: Nandini was probably surprised and a little embarrassed, realising the essay sounded furious without meaning to; there may also have been reluctant respect for the teacher's comment.

qa.q: What changes made the essay's tone work on paper?
qa.a: Nandini put the thesis in one plain sentence, added the steel-tumbler counterargument with an answer, and swapped harsh words like 'lazy' and 'obviously' for fairer ones.

qa.q: How might a reader who disagreed have felt reading the first draft?
qa.a: They would likely feel insulted at being called lazy and stop listening, even to strong evidence.

grounding: It shows a teenager building an essay with a thesis, evidence and counterargument, and learning that tone in writing is carried by word choice.

subtype: Personal writing and diaries as private space [Regulating]
passage:
Monday. After the fight over the cricket bat, Abhinav wrote in his notebook until his hand ached: I wish Omkar would just vanish for a year. He hid it under his mattress and felt calmer by dinner.
Wednesday. Omkar found the notebook while hunting for his charger, read that page and ran to Aai, half hurt, half triumphant. Abhinav's face burned. Aai read only the one line Omkar pointed to, then closed the notebook and handed it back. "Writing a feeling isn't doing it. This is yours. Omkar, you don't read it again." To Abhinav she added, "If something in there ever feels unsafe, bring it to me."
Saturday. Writing about the week, Abhinav noted that a player in his online game kept asking for his school name and had said, "don't tell your parents we chat." He stopped mid-sentence, stared at the line, then took the tablet to Aai. They blocked and reported the player together that evening.

qa.q: What did Abhinav write on Monday?
qa.a: Abhinav wrote: I wish Omkar would just vanish for a year.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when Omkar ran to Aai with the notebook?
qa.a: Abhinav felt exposed and ashamed, face burning, because a private angry line had been read; there may also have been fear of being taken literally.

qa.q: How did Aai balance privacy and safety?
qa.a: She read only the line shown, handed the notebook back, told Omkar not to read it again, and invited Abhinav to bring anything unsafe to her, which he did on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt reading 'vanish for a year'?
qa.a: Omkar was likely hurt by the line, which is partly why he ran to Aai, even though it was only anger written down.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a private notebook to sort out feelings, a parent respecting that writing is not acting, and a safety worry being taken to a trusted adult.
